item.title: Same Fraud Score, Different Decision
item.dc:creator: Samina Yasmin
item.description:
Code: github.com/Saminay786/transaction-risk-decision-framework · Status: in progress

What this project is about

Banks score every card transaction for fraud risk. But a score doesn’t stop fraud by itself. Someone still has to decide: approve the payment, send it to an analyst to review, or decline it.

This project builds that decision step. It combines the fraud probability, the transaction amount and the cost of each possible mistake, then picks the cheapest action for each transaction, without exceeding the number of reviews analysts can handle.

What to expect: a simple example of why a score isn’t enough, how each action is priced, four ways of deciding compared on unseen data, and how much we can trust the result.

How this differs from my IIT Madras project

I first worked on this problem in a coursework project at IIT Madras: Credit Default and Fraud Risk Prediction (American Express – IIT Madras, 2022). I cleaned the data, balanced the classes with SMOTE-Tomek, and compared seven models. XGBoost did best on ROC-AUC and F1.

That project asked “how risky is this case?” This one asks what a risk team needs next: “what do we do about it, and what will it cost?”

IIT Madras coursework This project
Output A risk score Approve, review or decline
Rare fraud cases Oversampled Left as they are, so probabilities stay realistic
Testing Random splits Train on the past, test on a later period
Judged by ROC-AUC, F1 € cost, fraud caught, customers affected

Two transactions, same score

A €3 coffee and a €900 laptop both get a 10% fraud score. The common rule, “decline if the score is above 0.5”, approves both.

But if the laptop is fraud, the bank loses €900 plus fees. An analyst check costs about €5, which is clearly worth it for the laptop and not for the coffee. Same score, different right answer.

How it works

Data. The public ULB credit-card dataset: 284,807 European card transactions over two days, 492 of them fraud (0.17%).

Model. LightGBM, trained on the first 60% of the timeline and tested on the last 20%, as it would be used in real life. Unlike my coursework project, I didn’t oversample fraud. Oversampling inflates the scores, so a “10%” stops meaning 10%. Here the probability feeds a € calculation, so it has to be honest.

Pricing each action. With p = fraud probability and A = amount:

approve = p × (A + fees)
review  = analyst cost + p × (share analysts miss) × (A + fees) + (1 − p) × customer delay
decline = (1 − p) × (lost margin + cost of an annoyed customer)

For the laptop: €92 to approve, €15 to review, €33 to decline, so it goes to review. For the coffee: €1.80 to approve, so it goes through. The cost inputs (€5 per review, 90% of fraud caught on review, and so on) are assumptions that a real bank’s Finance team would supply.

Four ways of deciding:

  • P0: approve everything (the cost of doing nothing)
  • P1: decline if p > 0.5 (the common default)
  • P2: two cut-offs, tuned on past data
  • P3: the cheapest action per transaction, within a review cap of 1%

Results

P1: decline if p > 0.5 P3: cheapest action
Cost per 1,000 transactions €89.8 €69.4
Share of fraud € stopped 49% 68%
Analyst reviews used 0 33 (of 569 allowed)

P3 wins by doing exactly what the laptop example suggests: it spends a few reviews on risky, expensive transactions that the 0.5 rule lets through.

How sure are we? The test period has only 75 frauds, so I resampled it 1,000 times. P3 beats approving everything in 99.7% of resamples, and beats the 0.5 rule in 85%. The second gain is promising but not proven: its 95% range is −€352 to €3,493. I’d use it to justify a pilot, not to promise savings.

A surprise. P2, the tuned cut-offs, did slightly worse than the plain 0.5 rule. It was tuned on just 33 frauds, so it mostly fitted noise. P3 has nothing to tune, which helps when fraud examples are scarce.

If analysts cost more? Raising the review cost from €1 to €20, P3 uses fewer reviews (133 down to 4), and its cost stays around €67–70 per 1,000, against €90 for the 0.5 rule.

Is this new?

No, not as an idea. Making decisions by expected cost is well established, and this project applies it rather than inventing it:

  • Cost-based thresholds: Elkan, The Foundations of Cost-Sensitive Learning (IJCAI 2001).
  • Cost-based fraud decisions, per transaction: Correa Bahnsen et al., Cost Sensitive Credit Card Fraud Detection Using Bayes Minimum Risk (ICMLA 2013), and their later work on example-dependent costs.
  • A “review” option beside yes/no: the reject option, formalised by Chow (1957, 1970).
  • Resampling distorts probabilities: Dal Pozzolo et al., Calibrating Probability with Undersampling for Unbalanced Classification (IEEE SSCI 2015). This is from the same ULB group that released the dataset.
  • Limited analyst capacity in fraud: Dal Pozzolo et al., Credit Card Fraud Detection: A Realistic Modeling and a Novel Learning Strategy (IEEE TNNLS 2018).

What this project adds is small and practical: it puts these pieces into one end-to-end pipeline, with three actions, amount-based costs, a review cap and a test on a later time period. It also reports how uncertain the gain is, which most public work on this dataset skips, and shows that tuned cut-offs can fail when fraud examples are few.

Limitations and next steps

The costs are assumptions, there are few frauds, and the data covers only two days with no customer IDs. Next, I’d move the same decision layer to the larger IEEE-CIS dataset, keep each customer in only one of training or testing, and simulate chargebacks arriving weeks later, as they do in practice.

The takeaway: a fraud model’s job is to estimate risk. Deciding what to do with that risk is a separate job, and it’s where most of the money is.

Full details, formulas and a one-page decision memo are in the GitHub repo.

item.title: Almost Half of Promo Sales Would Have Happened Anyway
item.dc:creator: Samina Yasmin
item.description:
Code: github.com/Saminay786/promo-optimization-engine

The 20%-off puzzle

A box of cereal goes 20% off and sales double, from 100 boxes to 200. Success?

Maybe not. That same week, the cereal was probably also on the front of the weekly flyer and on a display at the end of the aisle. Some of those 200 boxes would have sold anyway, just at a lower price. And some shoppers simply switched from the cereal next to it.

“Sales went up during the promo” mixes all of that together. Plan from it, and you keep paying for discounts that don’t earn their cost.

I used dunnhumby’s The Complete Journey, two years of real grocery shopping from about 2,500 households, to pull these apart in four steps:

Step Question Method
1. Measure How much extra does a discount actually cause? Double Machine Learning
2. Plan Which product gets which discount, in which week? Integer optimisation
3. Cross-check Does the whole-category view agree? Bayesian marketing mix model
4. Test Could a store test prove it works? A/B test simulation

Step 1: What does a discount really cause?

I built a weekly history for the 137 top-selling products over 99 weeks. Then I asked: in weeks when the discount was deeper than usual, beyond what the flyer, display, season and recent sales would explain, did sales rise more than expected? That’s the idea behind Double ML: strip out everything else first, so the discount only gets credit for what’s left.

Effect (θ) What 10% off does
Naive: promo weeks vs. normal weeks 3.49 +42% units
Double ML: other factors removed 2.51 (95% CI 2.18–2.85) +29% units
Placebo: discounts randomly shuffled 0.01 nothing, as it should

The naive view overstates the discount by about 40%, because it gives the discount credit for the flyer and display’s work. And 44% of promo-week sales would have happened anyway.

Step 2: Plan the promo calendar

For 8 weeks with 10 promo slots a week, which product should get 10%, 20% or 30% off, and when? The rules interact (a budget, a cap per category so cereals don’t steal from each other, no back-to-back weeks so shoppers don’t just stock up), so I set it up as an integer program and let a solver (OR-Tools CP-SAT) find the best combination.

The comparison is a common rule of thumb: deepest discount on the best sellers. Same rules, same $5k budget:

Extra margin Budget used
“Deepest discount on top sellers” $60 all of it
Optimised calendar $719 37% less

The rule of thumb loses because 30% off only pays for itself on about 1 in 4 products. On the rest, the discount given on sales that would have happened anyway outweighs the extra sales. The solver saves deep discounts for products that respond strongly, like beer and soft drinks.

Step 3: Zoom out to the whole category

Step 1 looked at products one at a time. As a check, I modelled weekly sales for 8 whole categories with a Bayesian marketing mix model (PyMC-Marketing). It has three levers (discount, flyer and display), and it allows for effects that linger a week or two and for diminishing returns.

  • Most discounts don’t pay for themselves. In 7 of 8 categories, each $1 of discount brings back less than $1 of margin. Soft drinks return about $0.69. Only frozen pizza clears break-even.
  • The twist: both models rank the categories the same way, but the category-level effect is only about half the product-level one. That’s what cannibalisation looks like: when one cereal is discounted, part of its jump is taken from the cereal next to it. The category total rises by less than the product does.
  • So Step 2’s $719 is probably about twice too high. The comparison still holds, since both plans use the same estimates, but the dollar figure is optimistic.

Step 4: Could a store test even prove it?

A prediction isn’t proof. So I designed the test a retailer would run: split stores 50/50, run the new calendar in half, and compare weekly promo margin, using CUPED (adjusting for how each store did before the test) to cut the noise. Then I simulated it 1,000 times on real store history:

  • The test is fair: with no real change, it raised a false alarm about 5% of the time, exactly as designed.
  • But it’s too small. With 84 usable stores, it reliably detects only lifts of about 13% or more. The calendar is expected to add about 3%, and this test would catch that only about 10% of the time.
  • CUPED roughly triples the chance of catching a real effect.

So a “not significant” result wouldn’t mean the calendar failed, only that the test couldn’t see it. Proving a 3% lift would need about 1,500 stores, a longer test or a less noisy metric. Much better to know that before running it.

What I’d tell a promo team

  1. Judge a promo by the sales it creates, not the sales it records. Almost half of promo volume was going to happen anyway.
  2. Deeper isn’t better. Most categories lost money on deeper discounts. Save them for the few products that really respond.
  3. Check product-level wins at category level. Part of every “uplift” is stolen from the shelf next to it.
  4. Size the test before you run it. Otherwise a “no effect” result can kill a good idea.

Limitations

The data is observational, so the Double ML result holds only if I’ve measured what drives both promo decisions and sales. There’s no cost data: margin (30% of price), supplier funding (50% of the discount) and display costs are assumptions. Cannibalisation and stock-piling are handled with simple rules. And with only a 2,500-household panel, a real retailer’s full store sales would make the test far more powerful.

Next: scale product-level effects to category level before optimising, model stock-piling directly, and compare other test designs, such as alternating weeks.

Full code, results and every number above are in the GitHub repo.
